title: Dreyfus
hookLine: a Jewish officer falsely convicted in France, and a writer who would not stay quiet

lines: A SWORD BROKEN IN A COURTYARD.
cards: A courtyard in Paris on a cold morning. Soldiers stand in a square. An officer is marched to the center, and in front of everyone the braid is torn from his uniform and his sword is broken.
He calls out that he is innocent. Beyond the railings a crowd jeers, and some of the shouting is not about spies at all, but about Jews. The officer is Captain Alfred Dreyfus.
He is Jewish, he is loyal, and he did not do it.

teach.b: France was proud of being the country of liberty, equality and fraternity, and its Jews were full citizens. Dreyfus was an officer on the army's general staff.
Then a secret note turned up: someone was passing military information to Germany. Suspicion fell on Dreyfus, on thin evidence, and a military court convicted him of treason.
He was shipped to a prison on Devil's Island, off South America. Later, evidence pointed to a different officer. The army protected that officer, and he was acquitted.
That's when the novelist Émile Zola wrote an open letter to the president of France, printed on a newspaper's front page under two huge words: J'accuse. I accuse.
He named the men he said had covered up the truth.

Zola was tried, convicted, and left the country. France split, families and friends arguing at dinner tables over one man. Dreyfus was brought back for a second trial and, astonishingly, convicted again.
Then he was pardoned, and only years later fully cleared and returned to the army. Why does this belong in a Jewish story?

Because the case showed that hatred of Jews had not disappeared in a modern, enlightened country; it could stand in a crowd in the capital. A young journalist from Vienna was in Paris covering the case.
And the Torah has a line for anyone who, like Zola, risks something to stop an injustice: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word is said twice.
Some teachers read the doubling as a call to pursue justice by just means, too.

how: Jewish teaching ties the pursuit of justice to the Torah's command, 'Justice, justice shalt thou follow', and the Dreyfus case is often taught as a lesson in standing up against a public falsehood.

games.q: you are Émile Zola, a well-known novelist. you believe an innocent Jewish officer is in prison and the army is hiding the truth. what do you do?
o: stay out of it and keep writing novels.
write privately to a friend in government.
publish an open letter naming those responsible.
games.why: Zola published J'accuse on a newspaper's front page. he was convicted for it and left France, but the case was reopened.

practice: Bring to mind one small unfairness near you: a rumor about someone, a person always blamed, a joke that lands on the same group every time.
Don't solve it yet; just look at it straight, the way Zola looked at the papers and said, this is wrong. Then let one small way of refusing to go along take shape: a word, a question, a quiet no.

wordCard.voice: Dreyfus. A Jewish officer in France, falsely convicted of treason, defended by Zola's J'accuse, and in the end cleared. Today's word.
